title: AI phone answering for bars and grills
seoTitle: AI phone answering for bar and grill phone orders | ROAL
description: See how AI phone answering can take pickup calls, answer menu questions, and send clean tickets to the kitchen for bars and grills.
question: How can I use AI phone answering for bar and grill phone orders without adding more work for my staff?
answer: An AI phone host can answer your bar and grill phone orders, take pickup and delivery details from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It can also answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions, while handing tricky calls to staff and never taking card numbers over the phone.
summary: You’ll see how to handle bar and grill phone orders with less phone chaos and a cleaner kitchen line.
intro:
Bar and grill phone orders can eat up a lot of time during lunch, happy hour, and dinner rush. An AI phone host can answer the phone, take the order, and pass a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

That matters because a lot of these calls are simple. People want wings, burgers, fries, a pickup time, and a quick answer about hours or parking. ROAL is built for that kind of call flow, especially when the front counter is busy and the phone keeps ringing.

sections.h2: What should an AI phone host do for a bar and grill?
sections.body:
For a bar and grill, the phone host should handle the repeat calls that slow your team down. That usually means pickup orders, delivery orders, hours, address, parking, and basic menu questions.

ROAL does those jobs from your live menu. It takes items, sizes, modifiers, and notes, then confirms the order back before sending a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also speaks the caller’s language, collects the caller’s name and phone, quotes a ready time, and can take reservation requests.

A practical script sounds like this:
- "Thanks for calling. What can I get started for you today?"
- "Do you want pickup or delivery?"
- "Any sauces, sides, or notes I should add?"
- "Your order will be ready at 6:20."

For a bar and grill menu, that means common calls like wings, burgers, wraps, salads, kids meals, and sides can move without a staff member stopping service to answer the phone. If someone asks about allergy-sensitive items or a manager request, the host passes that to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: How do bar and grill phone orders move from call to kitchen?
sections.body:
The cleanest setup is simple: phone rings, order is taken, ticket goes to the kitchen, and staff sees it on the screen. That is the main job of ROAL, and it keeps the handoff clear.

Here is the flow in plain steps:
1. A customer calls your restaurant.
2. The host greets them and checks whether they want pickup, delivery, or something else.
3. The host reads your live menu and takes the order.
4. The host confirms items, sizes, modifiers, and notes back to the caller.
5. The host collects name and phone, then gives a ready time.
6. The ticket lands on the kitchen screen.

Example: say your average bar and grill phone order is $28. If you get 12 completed phone orders in a month, that is 12 tickets sent to the kitchen. If you get 40, that is 40 tickets. Plug in your own order count and average check so you can see whether missed calls are costing more than the time you spend answering them.

A good checklist for your manager is:
- Make sure the live menu is current.
- Mark sold-out items clearly.
- Add your real hours and address.
- Decide which calls should go to staff right away.

sections.h2: How do I set it up without a big project?
sections.body:
Setup is designed to be quick for busy owners. You paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or even just "Name, City" at /try. ROAL reads your public menu pages, menu PDFs, menu photos, hours, and address, then builds a phone host in about a minute.

You can also upload a menu in any format. Before you go live, you can test-call it right in the browser, and there is no sign-up needed for that test step.

A simple owner checklist:
- Gather your website or Google Maps link.
- Check that hours and address are current.
- Make sure your menu photos or PDF are readable.
- Test the greeting, pickup flow, and menu accuracy.
- Pick the voice and name you want the host to use.

If you run multiple concepts or locations, ROAL also supports multi-location menus in the dashboard. That is useful when one site has a different lunch special or a different late-night menu. The goal is to keep the phone host aligned with what the kitchen can actually make.

sections.h2: How do I forward calls from my existing number?
sections.body:
You do not have to give up your restaurant number. When you claim the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it.

You can forward all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. Forwarding can be turned off any time, which is helpful if you want to test it during a rush shift first.

Common carrier and phone system setup often looks like this, but always confirm with your carrier and test with a call:

| Setup type | Common code or method |
| --- | --- |
| Many landlines and some carriers | *72 + forwarding number for all calls, *73 to turn off |
| AT&T and T-Mobile GSM mobile phones | **21*number# for all calls, ##21# to turn off |
| AT&T and T-Mobile GSM mobile phones | **61*number# for unanswered calls |
| AT&T and T-Mobile GSM mobile phones | **67*number# for busy calls |
| Verizon Wireless | *72 / *73 for all calls, *71 for busy/no-answer |
| Business VoIP systems | Set forwarding in the web portal |

That matters for bar and grill phone orders because you can keep your current number on the door, the menu, and Google, while the calls route where you want them. If you are unsure which code applies, confirm with the carrier or system provider before turning it on.

sections.h2: What should I do about pricing, payments, and tricky calls?
sections.body:
Bar and grill owners usually care about two things here: what it costs and what the host should not do. ROAL charges $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free, and billing happens monthly.

That can be easier to compare with other common models. Many AI phone tools charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599 whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can add up fast on a $24 or $35 tab.

For example, say a completed phone order is $0.90 and your average phone check is $30. If you get 50 completed orders, your cost is $45 for the month. Plug in your own average order size and call volume to compare it with your current phone handling costs.

Important limits:
- The host does not take card numbers over the phone.
- Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it.
- Sold-out items should not be offered.
- Allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering, and manager requests go to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: How does it help during rushes, late nights, and short staff?
sections.body:
The busiest phone hours at a bar and grill are usually the same hours your team is busiest in person. Lunch rush, after-work pickup, game nights, weekends, and late calls can all pile up at once.

A phone host can take the steady calls off the front counter so staff can focus on food and guests. That is where ROAL fits well for a place that sells wings, burgers, appetizers, and late-night takeout.

Use this quick playbook:
- During lunch, let the host handle standard pickup orders.
- During dinner rush, forward all calls or only busy calls.
- After hours, let the host answer hours, address, and the next opening time.
- If a caller asks for a manager, send that call to staff with a summary.

A good example line for a busy shift is: "I can take that order now, and I’ll have it ready at 7:10." That is short, clear, and easy for the caller to hear. If a customer starts asking about a large party, a catering tray, or a special request, the host can hand it to staff instead of guessing.

sections.h2: How should I test it before I trust it on the line?
sections.body:
Before you forward your main number, run a few test calls with real menu items and real problems. That tells you whether the host sounds natural and whether the kitchen ticket matches the way your team works.

Test these calls one by one:
1. A normal pickup order with fries and a drink.
2. A modified burger order with no onion and extra sauce.
3. A sold-out item to make sure it is not offered.
4. A question about hours, address, and parking.
5. An allergy-sensitive question that should go to staff.

Check the dashboard after each call. You should see call history with transcripts and recordings, plus live tickets marked new, preparing, or ready. You can also review menu editor notes, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus there.

If you want a quick starting point, [build a free test host from your website](/try) and use your own menu, not a generic example. ROAL is pre-launch, so the safest way to judge fit is to test your real menu and your real calls before you turn on forwarding.

faq.q: How do I forward my restaurant number to an AI phone host?
faq.a: You keep your current number and forward it to the phone line the host gets when you claim it. Many carriers and phone systems use codes or a portal for forwarding, but the exact steps vary by carrier and plan, so confirm with your provider and test with a call.

That can be easier to compare against monthly plans that charge whether or not orders come in.
